utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Our apologies for the late start this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Our apologies for the late start. I remind you the affirmation you made still applies. Now, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to begin this morning by asking you a few more questions about the notes and the Joint Command meetings or sessions that you attended in 1998. You have told us, I think, on Tuesday at page 8012 that when -- and yesterday at page 12 in particular, you said that when you were taking notes you "only jotted down those details and facts that I felt might be of use to my command in their assessment of the Siptar terrorist forces' strength." But that -- but you also wrote down additional things that were said by those attending the meeting, didn't you? We have several examples of the civilians talking about things that seem to deal with more than simply the strength of terrorist forces. Do you recall or should we look at some examples?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. There were additional matters that you are mentioning now that related to the protection of the civilians to supplies, assistance, to citizens of both Albanian and Serbian ethnicity, in terms of food stuffs and the daily problems that they had; but as a matter of course, this was something that Mr. Andjelkovic dealt with. As for the others, they took the floor as they felt that they should perhaps add something or participate in the discussion and so on. So yes, there were other matters and not only those that had to do with the Siptar terrorist forces' strength and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your discussion with Mr. Djurdjic about that matter in general on Tuesday, at page 8012 and following, you agreed with him generally when he asked you if it was fair to say that there wasn't a single minute where any decision had been ordered by the Joint Command when there was no decision issued by them or mentioned in your notes. And I want to ask you about the meeting of July 27th. And this is in Exhibit 886, and it's at page 15 of both the English and the B/C/S, the portion I want to ask you about. Mr. Djurdjic talked to you about this meeting, this was a meeting that was attended by General Samardzic and there were discussions about what the plan was going to be. And on page 15 the last speaker at the meeting is listed in your notes as Mr. Minic and he says: "Continue the plan at 0700 hours as agreed." Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Mr. Minic said that because the army commander was present and he advised -- he informed everyone that the plan was being implemented and then Mr. Minic in closing practically just reiterated what the army commander had already decided because the decision on the use of the forces was something that was made by the army commander, not by civilians. And Mr. Minic basically just reiterated his words that this plan from their perspective as it were, I don't know whether he was referring to the MUP or something else, but in any case, the commander, the army commander, had decided that the plan was to be implemented as of 0700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about a couple of -- couple of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can look at page 84 in the English, page 86 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This next one, General, is a meeting of the 10th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we'll have to rotate the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And near the bottom of that page you'll see Mr. Minic speaking and in my English translation among the things he says are: "Go into Dubovik and Radovic villages and see what the situation is like. Go into Prapacan village," says VJ, "and have the police occupy it." Skipping a bullet point, "Go into all villages and pressure them into handing over weapons. Secure the roads and control the territory. The army will adopt a plan on the arrangement of the territory on Monday. The MUP should do the same." Do you remember him saying all those things?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the gist of what he said for the most part. Whether I actually managed to write down every word that he actually said verbatim, I don't know, but for the most part it's as you have read out. What is he referring to there regarding the gathering of weapons, the collection of weapons, this was something that was on-going, and it was at the initiative of the command that this was undertaken but also at the initiative of the Albanian citizens who at this time were not willing -- or actually even as of September we had the situation where the citizens themselves were coming over, coming in to hand over their weapons, or they were handing in weapons, small quantities of weapons, but then holding back and keeping more sophisticated weapons with them. So we knew that this was really aimed at misleading the MUP into believing that they had already handed over their weapons. But there were also instances where entire quantities of weapons were handed over by village. For instance we even mortars handed over and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, let me stop there. I was just asking if you remember Mr. Minic saying all these things which on their face sound like they are in the nature of decisions or directions or instructions or orders, at least in the generic sense of those words? Do you remember him saying those things? You wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did write that down and that is the sense of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you answered Mr. Djurdjic on Tuesday about this, I think you're thinking -- well, let me ask you this: Are you thinking of the words "decision" and "order" in the technical military sense of something formal that you draft up and it has specific language in it and it's signed? Is that what you're thinking of when you say nobody in the Joint Command ever ordered the VJ to do anything out of these Joint Command meetings? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it. And I can confirm that that's how it was in terms of decisions. As for initiatives, I'm not denying that certain individuals took some initiative. However, that was not binding on the corps commander or the commander of the MUP staff in the sense that they would have had to implement that, but they could bear it in mind as a bit, a piece of information that they would be aware of when they were making their decision. So that is the sense of what is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did those kind of things expressed by Mr. Minic - and in the minutes there are other similar statements by Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Makovic at various meetings. I understand you're saying those were not binding on the corps, but in your experience did those kind of things carry weight with the corps? The fact that Mr. Minic or Mr. Sainovic or Mr. Makovic had said, Let's go there, let's do that; did that carry weight with the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a civilian, for instance, insisted on an issue, it was General Pavkovic's duty to relay that to General Pavkovic to inform him of the problem at a meeting, and then the commander would decide whether he would accept the proposal or initiative that was put forth by one of the gentlemen who were there or not. There were instances where the commander of the army would accept them fully. There were other instances where he would deny them or turn them down completely. And there were cases where he would take them into account for a certain part, especially when -- so the commander was really the one who had the final say especially when the use of the army was at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about with regards to the use of the MUP or do you know? Was the effect the same or did the MUP give more weight to what Mr. Minic and Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Makovic might say in the nature of a direction or instruction or an order? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that if there was a MUP unit of involved, the army commander, in view of the fact that the army provided support to the MUP, we had to advise him and inform him of the problem that had to do with the MUP unit, and then the commander would, in keeping with his decision, determine which forces to use as far as support was concerned. But as a matter of principle, he did not deny providing support except he never allowed the army to be used without the MUP units being used as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think two more -- two or three more I'd like to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 120 in the English and 123 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a meeting of 5 October 1998. And I guess -- when did you stop taking the minutes -- or taking the notes and you were replaced by your subordinate Tesevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approximately around the 20th, so I took notes at some 65 meetings, and the last five the notes were taken by Colonel Tesevic. I think this was around the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So on the 5th of October, this is another one that you would have been taking the notes. Mr. Sainovic is noted as saying: "Our operations should be commensurate with the number" and "we should go to minor or small-scale actions." And then next he says: "The leaders should be liquidated now that we have enough information. Go with everything in order to deal with individuals." Do you recall what he was talking about in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it. There were discussions about some individuals who were member of the command personnel who were found to be some of the leaders of the terrorist uprising in Kosovo, especially among them a sultan from Ovcarevo and Ramus Haradinaj in the area of Baranski Lug and in the Junik mountains. They were not mentioned by name then, but this relate -- referred to those leaders of the extremist ideology, and the gentlemen from state security were talking at this meeting about being in pursuit of these individuals and that they were trying to capture them and if not, then that they should liquidate them in combat. And I assume that Mr. Sainovic, based on the information that General Pavkovic provided regarding the handing over of weapons in certain villages and the reports of the MUP, he was probably stressing this particular problem which had already earlier been pointed to by state security organs, and he probably felt that the key issue was to separate the terrorists as soon as possible from the civilian population. And if that -- if they were to be successful in that, that then there wouldn't be much opposition among the civilian population in returning to their homes and staying there. So I'm just basically para-phrasing what he said then, but I do recall the meetings where this was under discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, 121 of the English, 124 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that same meeting near the bottom of the page you'll see Mr. Sainovic talking again; three bullet points, the third one says: "DB operatives - liquidate individuals." DB is the state security; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your last answer you suggested that this talk about liquidating individuals was in combat. It doesn't say "in combat." Wasn't this just a matter of finding these leaders and killing them? In combat or any other way? I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part of Mr. Hannis's question also contains certain conclusions that are not actually valid, but in the latter part of his question he actually corrected himself, so I don't really have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary; the question is clear. Yes, I did mention combat operation, but this does not preclude the use of units in combat operations. For instance, we had the case where sultan was attacked. His commanding of Carevo was assaulted. And some combat elements captured of Carevo and not state security organs. State security organs and being a member of the military security organ, I know this, their responsibility was to discover the leaders of terrorist activities in their operative work. And when those individuals actually offer resistance during their attempt to arrest them, then they could use their weapons. And of course in that sense Mr. Sainovic is here commenting the comments put forth by Mr. Radovic and Mr. Gajic because they frequently reported that they were in pursuit of certain terrorists. But there was never an instance where they reported that there was any fighting or that they had caught someone. And I recall a meeting where Mr. Radovic said that a Siptar had been liquidated and this man was someone for whom the Albanians had discovered that he had ties with the state security service and apparently he provided them certain information. However, they themselves learned that some information that he provided in relation to the mass grave in Klecka where remains, human remains, were found; and on the basis of what I learned then, these were human remains of Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'd like to do, if it's not opposed by counsel and if it's agreeable to Your Honours, is rather than go through several other points that I'd like to bring to your attention I would simply name the pages where I think there are examples of the civilian members of the Joint Command talking about things that on the face appear to be in the nature of directions, orders, instructions. For your future reference when you are considering the issue I would just list the pages where they occurred on and move on or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with my learned colleague and I trust that his quotations will be accurate, but let's not overdo it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic is having an each-way position. Mr. Hannis, proceed as you proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, Your Honours, I would suggest that examples of this can be found at page 130 of the English, 13 October meeting, Mr. Sainovic speaking. At page 128 of the English, 11 October, again Mr. Sainovic speaking twice on that first page. On page 125 of the English, 8th of October meeting, Mr. Sainovic. The 7th of October meeting on 124 of the English, Mr. Sainovic. We talked about that one. Page 112 of the English, 26 September, 1998 meeting, Mr. Sainovic. Page 113, 29th of September, Mr. Minic speaking. 22 September 1998, page 108, Mr. Sainovic speaking. And finally I think one in August that I'd like to bring to your attention. The 1st of August, at page 27 of the English, Mr. Matkovic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to talk to you a little bit further about the nature of the interaction between the Joint Command and the VJ. And I'd like you to have a look at P1229. I think you talked about this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have a hard copy if the Usher could hand it to you. It's a two-page document, so that may help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a 29 September 1998 document authored by and sent from General Pavkovic to the 3rd Army command personally to the commander. The title is "Implementation of Stage 5 of the Plan." You've looked at this one before, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to item number 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's on page 2 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You find that? My English translation reads as follows: "During the briefing on the course of implementing stage five of the plan which was given at the meeting of the ZK." And in this context I take it ZK means "Zajednicka Komanda," Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "... at the meeting of the Joint Command for Kosova-Metohija on 10 September 1998, the other command organs pointed out that the VJ had not carried out two of its duties under the plan. Namely, number 1, it had not formed rapid intervention helicopter units as the FRY president had ordered at the meeting on 31 August 1998; and 2, two BGs, battle groups, had not been moved down to Kosovo and Metohija." Did you see this document in 1998? Did you know General Pavkovic had written it to General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you remember this matter being discussed at a Joint Command meeting on the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My question is in this paragraph where General Pavkovic says: "The other command organs at the Joint Command meeting pointed out that the VJ hadn't carried out its duties." I understand that the MUP would be another command or organ, but this says other command organs in the plural. Who besides the VJ and the MUP would be a command organ that's participating in the Joint Command meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimonies both last year and this year I repeatedly said that there were only two organs where I was. They were the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps staff command, and they were responsible for coordinating the work based on the decision of the army commander. I never denied that there were also representatives of the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there as well as representatives of Serbia. As you mentioned there yourself, there were these four individuals who had frequently attended these meetings of, as it says there, the Joint Command. Whom General Pavkovic actually was referring to here, I wouldn't know. But I know that he considered other organs to be mainly the MUP command or the MUP staff because they were the ones who were supposed to take part in the creation of these intervention units. But I also believed that he probably meant the other civilian representatives from the federal and republic governments because General Pavkovic sometimes referred to them as the Joint Command. I can only reiterate my claim now that they did not take any decisions, the decisions were taken in Belgrade; and they probably informed President Milosevic either through phone calls or in person how the activities were evolving, developing. And then based on that, he would make a decision on the use of forces and issue orders to the Chief of the General Staff and the MUP staff. I am certain that these civilians who came down there to Kosovo were very fair in their treatment of the commands. They never insisted on anything being implemented. But as you were saying or pointing out, they had some sway by providing -- by offering their initiatives and opinions, they had some sway with the commanders to take them into account in their decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what you just described as that sway related in part to their relationships with Mr. Milosevic; would you agree with that statement? That's what gave them weight?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was a technical error. The wrong channel was on. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We missed that answer. Would you be able to tell us again what you were saying, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to repeat. I know that the gentlemen from the authorities of the federal republic and the Republic of Serbia were in touch from time to time with President Milosevic, and I know they occasionally travelled to Belgrade and I suppose they met with him also. But what they discussed, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more thing on this document down near the bottom of the page, immediately above the words "we propose." General Pavkovic says: "Moreover, we are giving the members of the ZK, Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, the opportunity to report to the president of the FRY that the VJ has not carried out its duties under the plan." Do you know why General Pavkovic inserted that in this document to General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic is letting the army commander know that he too had attended the meeting with the president when the problem was discussed. And he reminds him that the problem with the creation of helicopter units and bringing in two combat groups into Kosovo had practically been approved by President Milosevic's plan, but that assignment had not been carried out. And he warns that members of the Joint Command are reminding everyone, and he is informing the army commander in writing of this problem. Now, what is Joint Command here? We know that in Belgrade everybody is there with President Milosevic. There is some sort of intersectorial command or staff - I don't know what they call it in their minutes. And all those members working in Kosovo were at the same time participating in Belgrade in that intersectorial command. They were just sent on a mission to Kosovo to provide the president with some factual information that could contribute to making political decisions because what is discussed here is the political situation, not combat with Siptar terrorists. If it had been ordered to neutralise all the forces in Kosovo, I think the army would have achieved that within seven to eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to refer to you another document that is sort of related to this continuing issue between General Pavkovic and General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D212. I think it's just one page, so if you'll have a look at it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is dated the 5th of October, 1998. And I see what appear to be your initials on the lower left. Is this the one that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have Pavkovic writing to General Samardzic, item 2, he says: "The plan to smash the DTS sabotage forces on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija authorised by the president stipulated that when the DTS had been smashed by the MUP and VJ forces rapid intervention forces shall be formed to be at full readiness, with the engagement of MI-8 helicopters to intervene at threatened sectors and features, as ordered by the President. "On my return from the reporting session with the ZK," Joint Command, I assume, "on 19 and 20 September, 1998, I informed you personally by telephone of the decision to form rapid-intervention forces." When he speaks there of the decision to form these forces, he is talking about a decision of the Joint Command, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is talking about Mr. Milosevic's decision at state level. So it's not the Joint Command. The Joint Command, or rather, one of its member, perhaps even General Pavkovic, proposed that rapid-intervention forces be formed and that proposal was submitted to the president. And based on that briefing, that reporting, that was done by General Pavkovic on behalf of the army and someone else on behalf of the MUP, he, the president, decided that forces should be created dedicated to rapid intervention, so as to be ready in case of emergency to act quickly so as not to have -- to engage larger army forces. These rapid-intervention forces with some helicopters, perhaps, would be sent immediately to a particular sector to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The next sentence says: "As part of the conclusions from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija meeting, I sent you the decision to form rapid-intervention forces..." What decision is he talking about, and what conclusions from the Joint Command is he talking about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what he is talking about here because he mainly dictated to me. I did type it out, he did make some corrections, but most of this document I wrote myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look then at the Joint Command meeting for the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is P886. At page 105 -- or 105 of the English, 109 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see, that's for the meeting on the 20th of September, but I need to take you to the last entry from that meeting which is actually on page 110 of the B/C/S and 106 of the English. The speaker is Mr. Sainovic, and in my English translation he is noted as saying: "Prepare and train the units for quick interventions. Form groups and then /?/ ask the air force to send helicopters, prepare the task and plan." And then on Thursday it's scratched out, it says Friday. "The commanders of the helicopter units commanders to come at 1000 hours and an army operations officer." That appears to be the only noted reference to helicopters and intervention units in that meeting, and it's Mr. Sainovic at the conclusion of the meeting making those comments? So is that what's referred to in General Pavkovic's communication to General Samardzic that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. From what I understand, I don't rule out the possibility that Mr. Sainovic had contacted President Milosevic to discuss the issue. I don't rule out that possibility because here he puts forward certain details that he may have personally learned from the president about the creation of these units. I don't believe Mr. Sainovic was deciding on his own. His practice was to travel to Belgrade to meet with the president personally, and I don't rule out the possibility that the president had given him very specific tasks to tell General Samardzic such and such a thing and then that he, in keeping with his own powers, make the decision on the use of forces. Mr. Sainovic did not have the right, nor did he ever try to order Samardzic or Pavkovic anything. But he must have seen President Milosevic to share with him his opinions about the creation of that unit in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think I'm done with Joint Command notes for now. I wanted to ask you about a document that you were shown yesterday. This is Exhibit D324. If you can have a look at the on screen. It's a document dated 1st of August, 1998, from General Pavkovic to the 3rd Army. And it's a request for approval to launch the third stage of the plan. My question deals with the document itself. We have what appears to be the signature of General Pavkovic and a stamp, but there's no -- nothing else on it in terms of what we often see in other VJ documents. There are no initials of the author or -- and the typist, and there's no delivery information. There's no archival stamps that we sometimes see when the documents have been retrieved from the VJ archives. Is that unusual? Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing particularly unusual because as far as these activities around Ovcarevo are concerned, I've already described that. This was followed by activities around Liko vac, Ovcarevo, and combat actions. This is a command of the Pristina Corps sending to the forward command post of the 3rd Army; General Pavkovic was sending it to the forward command post of the 3rd Army. Whether it was handed in to someone in person, I don't know why they did not register it. But we see the designations, the -- and the signature of General Pavkovic; we see that he signed it himself, how he had it transmitted. He could have handed it to someone. Now, whether the 3rd Army registered it in a log-book, it was up to them. Because you have seen that document that concerns General Djordjevic, it was shown him on the 18th of April. General Pavkovic handed it on to the competent office for registration only two days later, so it must have been a simple omission and the same thing is possible here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You were asked, I think, yesterday at page 8 about Mr. -- by Mr. Djurdjic about who was in charge of the MUP units or the MUP units in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, and you gave an answer about 1998 regarding Mr. -- General Lukic and the MUP staff. Do you know why General Djordjevic and General Stevanovic were attending Joint Command meetings in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can hardly answer the direct question. I can only give you my impressions about their engagement there in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you can't answer, that's fine. Let me ask that next question: Do you know who in the MUP was responsible for sending PJP units from outside Kosovo to Kosovo in 1998 and in 1999? Do you know who that person would have been?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard from General Pavkovic, it was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that for 1998 and 1999 both?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so because in 1998 at all meetings with the president, Mr. Vlajko attended as the most senior officer in the Ministry of Interior, and without his decision, units of the ministry could hardly be sent to Kosovo in any scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked about how often you saw General Djordjevic in Kosovo after October 1998. I think your answer was you just saw him that one time at the meeting on or about the 18th or 19th of April. How about General Lukic? Did you see him in Kosovo in 1999, and if so, how often?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to meetings and it's true that I saw Mr. Djordjevic and Lukic and Obrad Stevanovic on the 18th of April. I knew Lukic was there; I heard that from other people because I was no longer involved in any coordination in 1999. I don't know about Obrad. And about Mr. Djordjevic, I don't know either. And I did not see either him or Mr. Obrad Stevanovic, and I do not know whether they came there or not. During proofing, I was asked about the 1st of June, but what I know, I know from double hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I want to look at Exhibit 340. This was shown to you yesterday by Mr. Djurdjic. And I have a hard copy for you because it's several pages. If the Usher could help me with that. Thank you. D340.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is at 2nd October, 1998, analysis of task executed on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija from the 3rd Army. Do you remember looking at this before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to, first of all, page 4 in the English. And it's page 3 for you, General. Item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It talks about experiences gained. And my first question relates to the positive experiences. You see the last item under positive experiences, my English translation reads as follows: "The distribution of weapons to citizens loyal to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia," and then in parentheses it says, "of Serbian and Montenegrin ethnicity has made it possible for large-scale resistance against the terrorist to be organised." So was it only Serbian and Montenegrin citizens in Kosovo that were being provided weapons in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 all the citizens except Albanians received as part of the general mobilisation or partial mobilisation weapons that they were entitled to by establishment. I said that two days ago. And in the Ministry of Defence, units of the civilian protection and civilian defence were also given weapons including members of other ethnicities to protects their own lives and property and local communes in villages and hamlets. There were several attempts to create some mixed Serb/Albanian units in Kosovo Polje. One of these attempts was made by Mr. Pesic who was commander of the military district. However, the response from the Albanian community was not great, and he did not succeed in creating any mixed units. The Albanian community refused outright to receive weapons and to put up any resistance to the terrorists in Kosovo. If you ask me what the reason was, I think that many of them supported separatism but many others also feared reprisals, revenge, including torture by other ethnic Albanians if they joined the army and the police in any kind of effort whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me jump ahead to a related document right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P889.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is on the issue of armed non-Siptars in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I never asked the General anything on this subject. Mr. Hannis could have dealt with it in direct examination if he had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it arises from his use of that document which has negative aspects of -- positive and negative aspects of what the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps had done in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it flows, in your submission, from the use of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, this is General Lazarevic's 16th February document that you've seen before. And in item 2 - in the English at page 4 and in your B/C/S I think we need page 3 - there's reference to the Pristina Corps task and it talks about engaging the non-Siptar population. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found that. Oh I see it. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who that refers to? That -- so that would not be members of the MUP or members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to something I've already explained. Serbs, Montenegrins, Muslims, the Roma, and other people who were vulnerable and undefended in Serbian villages, where they suffered from frequent Siptar terrorists attacks, and where the army and the MUP were unable to assign forces to protect villages. Therefore, as part of the general measures, such population was equipped and armed to protect their own lives and property. And these were people aged 65 to 80, the elderly, and children. Those who were not mobilised, who were not subject to mobilisation and who were certainly not capable of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in relation to that, if you'll go a little farther down, in response to your answer about using the forces to protect villages, do you see where it says -- talks about using those forces to protect non-Siptar villages? Or places with non-Siptar populations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean this part of the text which says: "... and also for the protection of villages with non-Siptar population ."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm trying to tell you. The army and the MUP were unable to detach any stronger forces to protect the population because they had their main task to carry out. For the army to protect the population, it would have had to dedicate at least a platoons or company-size units, and we were unable to afford that because we were busy protecting roads. And in order to protect that population somehow, within the effort at the level of the Ministry of Defence, they were given certain weapons in addition to some weapons they already had from earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But what about protecting Siptar villages with loyal Siptars?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Places where loyal Siptars lived were perfectly accessible to the army and the MUP, and the units could be deployed there just as easily as in Serbian villages. And we did not have any problems there such as attacks on units until 1999. There were no attacks of the population against our units. You have reports that I wrote signed by General Pavkovic sent to armoured brigades instructing units how to treat the population. Those commanders spoke to the seniors in villages and they reached some sort of understanding. But when these elders were replaced by younger men, these understandings were no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I personally ran across columns of Albanians who were leaving their own villages for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you back to D340. And it's on page 3 of the B/C/S version. And page 3 of the English. The report includes information about the number of terrorists that were killed or liquidated in my translation here. It says a total of 1299. And I guess this is in the period up to the 1st or 2nd of October. You saw the -- you saw the document of the minutes of the meeting that took place on the 29th of October, 1998, in Belgrade where General Pavkovic had reported on the work of the Joint Command. And in that report I will tell you that he reported that between the 25th of July and the 29th of October, that 3500 [Realtime transcript read in error "33500"] were killed, another 560 were liquidated, referring to terrorists, and another 666 were liquidated in the border area. That's a total of about 4700. Is it possible that 3400 terrorists were killed between the 1st and 29th of October during joint VJ and MUP actions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can say with certainty is that this -- these are not accurate details and accurate data regarding the deaths on the other side. And the reason is that in 1998 we almost never found Albanians who had been killed in combat. So we concluded that they most probably collected these bodies and took them out to their territory so that the commanders when preparing our reports and also our reports which we prepared for General Pavkovic for his briefing to the commander of the army and the Chief of General Staff and the president, we used figures that were just assessments of what their losses would have been. And that is possible in the army based on some indicators that you have during combat operations. So we didn't really know how many casualties they had. Me myself, I did not even see five dead Albanians. Perhaps I did see one person once in a barracks in Djakovica and maybe by the roadside as I travelled on the road. So I didn't see any other bodies. In other words, we just made assessments and the most accurate data on their casualties was the data we had from the border area because they left their bodies behind on these occasions and then these bodies were taken to Djakovica and handed over to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I think you answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, because of our delayed start -- I am sorry, I see Mr. Djurdjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 24, line 5, there is the figure of 33500. If you can just take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: An extra zero has been added.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I actually meant to say 3500, I think is what's in the document at that point. 3500 plus 560 plus 666. If I may, Your Honours, because of our late start, I don't know what time we'll be stopping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm holding on in the expectation that you may finish shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I can finish in the next 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to this document, you agreed to a question from Mr. Djurdjic about the -- whether or not there were any indications in this Exhibit D340 of any problems with the Pristina Corps not abiding by the commands of the 3rd Army, et cetera. But as of October 1998, were you aware that there indeed had been some complaints at the higher levels in the VJ about the use of the Pristina Corps units? And I'm talking specifically about at the General Staff level with General Perisic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned that from General Pavkovic. In other words, on the basis of a few letters and exchange of instances where information was exchanged between General Pavkovic and Samardzic, I noticed that General Samardzic, although he attended the meetings with President Milosevic and the Chief of General Staff and the chief of the security administration, once he went back to Pristina he tried to suppress, sort of, initiatives that were -- and that was not acceptable in the army because without something coming from the commander in the -- it could not be really implemented. So he tried to -- General Pavkovic tried to resolve this in his contacts with General Samardzic. But from what I heard on one occasion, General Perisic and Dimitrijevic in late September and early October began to stress this issue of Joint Command and all of a sudden that surfaced as an issue, emerged as an issue. Whereas throughout this period of July through August in 1998, they knew that civilians were in Kosovo, there were Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic, and others; and on one occasion I even heard from a man that General Perisic proposed - and I cannot claim that this is accurate - but I heard this a few months earlier, that he himself, he personally proposed that Mr. Andjelkovic be there. I personally did not attend these meetings, but I do not exclude that possibility. I can only assume why this proposal was put forth, but I can claim that General Dimitrijevic and General Perisic knew of this and all of a sudden this issue emerged as a problem and was emphasised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was a problem as early as July of 1998 with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was any issue with General Perisic in July, but I know that there was some pressure put on General Samardzic because I cannot see why General Samardzic would actually try to undermine a decision by the president which was made at the meeting where he was present. But in a way, he was actually seeking to accomplish something that had not been agreed at this meeting with President Milosevic in Belgrade. So my only conclusion was that there was a certain pressure put on General Samardzic to proceed in this way, in the way that General Perisic felt that it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In October, November, December, 1998, did you have any involvement or engagement in dealing with the KVM personnel from the OSCE in trying to carry out the terms of the October Agreements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of an incident that happened in December 1998, in and around Podujevo, which the OSCE, KVM, were pointing to as being a violation of the agreement where a VJ unit was engaged? Do you know the one I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain that I know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The VJ argued that it was just a training exercise and that they were attacked and then they returned fire. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this must have been in the area of Batalovo Lake if that's the incident you are referring to. Because we had training grounds there in the area of Batalovo Lake, and this is where a unit of the 15th Armoured Brigade actually had their training. And we had rotation of troops every three months because we had to provide training to the troops in an organised manner; we couldn't do it in barracks. But for the most part there were training grounds close to the garrison. They would have two or three training grounds. And each of those would have one shooting range.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you're not aware that there were discussions at the General Staff level concerning that in which General Dimitrijevic suggested that this was not a genuine training exercise but a provocation of the -- by the VJ of the KLA, and there were discussions involving the Joint Command and Mr. Sainovic's role in using VJ units? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. But I would like to clear something up, and I feel this is very important. Since the arrival of the OSCE Mission up until the end of the year, and I'm referring to 1998, there were 500 instances of attacks on representatives of the Ministry of the Interior and civilians. And as of May 1st -- as of January 1st and up until the beginning of the aggression, there were 652 instances. Now, the claim that the army was the one who actually engaged in provocations, that's untrue, because the army had no intention of provoking the Albanian terrorist forces unless they were conducting an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm running out of time. And the point I was inquiring about was whether you were aware that there had been discussions at the General Staff level of concerns about Mr. Sainovic's role, a civilian, in using or having an influence on how VJ units were used. I just -- two or three more areas to cover with you, General, and then I will be done. This is regarding the subordination order from General Ojdanic. And I had a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If he we could look first at P887.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see that one? It has a 3rd Army command number at the top, 872-94/2. It's dated the 19th of April. But the text of it seemed to be basically just General Ojdanic's order from the Supreme Command staff. Was this just simply forwarded on to the 3rd Army forward command post and the Pristina Corps? There seems to be no other information other than just General Ojdanic's order.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this is perfectly clear, this is an order by General Ojdanic issued to the commander of the 3rd Army and then he is drafting his own order and forwarding it to General Lazarevic, so they should approximately be the same. He is not allowed to change it. If a commander of the General Staff issued an order, then he would re-issue a similar order to the commander of the 3rd Army, and then he can actually expand it and make it more precise for the units in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The question I'm -- the point I'm trying to get at has to do with the numbering. I see this is 872-94/2 which, as I understand the system, would indicate this is like the second document related to that specific topic. And it's dated the 19th of April. If you could look next at D204, and this is a document dated the 20th of April. It appears that you were the author by the initials. And we see General Pavkovic's signature and stamp. And it bears the number 872-94/1. So I am confused. This seems to have the lower number indicating it was done earlier, and yet it's sent apparently a day later. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to refer back to the number of the document. So it's 872-94. Could I just see the number of the first -- the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me give you a hard copy of both of them so you can look at them side by side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered this question yesterday. So we have a situation General Pavkovic held on to this telegram. He kept it for himself. And that is why it appears as if this first order was signed and then only subsequently filed. In other words, the person who was on duty at the command post first filed this, and then once he had done that probably General Pavkovic came up to him and asked him to also file this document that he was working on. So what happened is, he was probably unable to make -- enter this correction because then he would have to scratch everything out and also he would have to stamp those scratches. So we can see based on this that there is an order, then there is a response from the army commander, and an order that he had drafted in connection with the order received from the General Staff. Yes, there was an error in the order in which these documents were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. From looking at those two documents, are you able to determine when you at the 3rd Army received General Ojdanic's order? Is there any information on there that would indicate when it came in, what date, what time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the resubordination order?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that this order arrived before 1730 hours on the 18th of April. It is certain that it arrived before that dead-line. How much earlier we can establish on this basis of this document that was received, the incoming stamp which says 1640 hours. I've just noticed that now, that it was received at this time. So what we have here is the General Pavkovic, after an hour later practically, he called the MUP organs and told them that an order had been received on their resubordination. And yesterday I explained why this was done -- why he did this on the 19th, because he probably kept this document for himself and then it was subsequently filed. So we can see on the basis of this stamp - and there cannot be any error here - where we see this incoming stamp which says it was received at 1640 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me be clear, if I understand your prior testimony, was the meeting that you and Pavkovic and Lazarevic then had with Djordjevic, Lukic, and Obrad Stevanovic the same day or the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was on the same day. I did not receive that document, but I think it was -- it must have been on that same day because I don't think that General Pavkovic - and I know him well - I don't think that he would have waited until the next day to provide this information. But I can see now on this incoming stamp that the time noted there is 1640 which actually confirms what I said, the meeting was about 5.30, 1730, which was, in other words, about an hour after the document was received. Because the incoming stamp, the code system that is used, it would note even the minute when the -- when a telegram arrives. Had it been 1642 minutes, it would have said so in the document there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any other question for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you something about certain irregularities you mentioned yesterday. It's on page 44 of the transcript of yesterday. In the 3rd Army command, you discussed certain irregularities in conducting combat operations, and you were asked if these informations you received from units, would you have to refer this to the higher, to your superiors. And you answered, Yes, this had to be done on the basis of the corps units and independent units. That sounds that these have been the rules and the regulations. Do you remember if at any stage these such reports were received by your -- by you or by your colleagues about irregularities in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified both on this occasion and last year, I talked about our having received a report from the commanders of the 125th and 549th Brigades, that there were certain problems in implementing these decisions because the competent organs of the civilian police units had not received an order from the MUP staff which had been coordinated at the Joint Command, this cooperation. So as long as the police units did not receive approval from General Lukic that they could conduct combat operations together with the army regardless of the army commanders' decision, those operations were not conducted. And in my view, that was the greatest error that was made because that cooperation had not taken effect and it did not work in practice. Although, I can state that it wasn't really that the police units refused to participate. Rather, they were just waiting for an order from the MUP staff to arrive, and once that happened, there were no problems of that kind anymore. As for irregularities in the field, I can only deduce that from some information that we received from time to time, but not in the sense that this was a major problem. What I assume is that the brigade commanders and the lower level commanders were probably better acquainted with the problems in the fields. I could only analyse the situation within units based on their reports, and based on those I would propose to General Pavkovic what measures to take and send to lower commands. Now, there were some reports, there was -- I found a report, for instance, about two Albanian civilians having been killed in Kosovo Polje by three members of the 37th Motorised Brigade who had come to Kosovo Polje from Srbica and killed those people. And the command was informed of this incident, measures were taken, the general ordered Colonel Stojanovic to apprehend these men, arrest them. They -- an investigation was conducted, but I don't know what the outcome was. In other words, an investigation was conducted into their actions. The same is true regarding the incident with the killings in Lipljani, and of course I'm just talking about the incidents that -- where there was army involvement, because I couldn't speak about any reports with the MUP. Now, had they been subordinated to us, then we would have received reports from them in the same way that we received reports from the 125th, 549th, and 15 Brigades. Simply put, we did not have any MUP combat reports on their participation because their reports were sent to the MUP staff. That's all that that means. And the MUP staff was the one who then decided how to use MUP units whereas the army role at this time was exclusively to provide support to MUP units. And I've already explained this, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you receive reports of this kind from units subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports, regular combat reports, but no. When I learned of some events and incidents that have come to light today, I can see the link; and you have been shown one document here where General Pavkovic, in regular intervals in seven to ten days after a certain stage of combat operations, ordered that a detailed report be submitted on the activities of the army and the MUP on the ground focusing on the execution of combat activities and possible irregularities, if any, or any other deviations from the orders. In those summary reports - because that's what we call them, summary reports - there was no specific knowledge provided by brigade commanders and commanders of independent brigades. And there was a curious case, if you allow me to tell you, in Zegra village when in 1999 Colonel Stojanovic informed General Pavkovic that in Zegra one ethnic Albanian family had been liquidated by members of the reserve force of the 175th Infantry Brigade based in Gnjilane. Instantly, General Pavkovic ordered me, Djakovic, we're going to Gnjilane now. I have to replace that brigade commander. I knew the man, this Colonel Petrovic, from earlier on. He was a very decent officer who certainly wouldn't have allowed anything like that to happen if he had any control, but he did not have control because that unit had just been mobilised. And included about 4.000 reservists. And I can understand the man. He was not able to achieve complete control at all levels within just a few days. So General Pavkovic immediately replaced the brigade commander and a few other senior officers, and a prosecution was started for this crime. I believe these reservists were convicted and sentenced to several years' imprisonment for the killing of civilians in Zegra village. That's the information I had and the command had as well. Now, in all other matters, I know that the corps command and the army command did take measures. We reacted to every report. There must have been deviations from orders, but commanders were not always apprised of everything and were not always able to take steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: General, that concludes the questions for you. I'm pleased to be able to tell you that you may now continue with your ordinary activities and you are no longer required here for further questions. We thank you for your attendance and the assistance that you've given us, and a Court Officer will assist you when we rise. We now adjourn, and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You stand for a reason, Mr. Djurdjic? Is there a procedural matter, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have two matters. The first one is an oral application to add some exhibits to our exhibit list. These are 65 ter 05346 and two zeroes 5350. They are five US KDOM reports. Four of them are dated December 1998 and relate to events in the area of Podujevo. The fifth one is dated January 1999 and it relates to events in the village of Racak that month. These reports are contemporaneous reports prepared by the US KDOM and relate directly to the evidence that this witness will be providing regarding these two events, so we seek to add them as we -- it is our position that these documents will assist the Chamber in understanding the witness's evidence on these matters. These exhibits have already been disclosed to the Defence both in English and B/C/S. They -- we became aware of their availability as public documents on Monday when the witness came for proofing. In discussions with him, he informed us that all US KDOM reports from that period are now available publicly in the US Department of State website. Previously these documents had been classified documents and were US Rule 70 documents. I should point out these quite specific reports, these five reports, had not been provided to us in the past. So they are new documents for us as well. And we have alerted the Defence to the fact that all this documentation is available on the website in the event that there may be also Rule 68 material in these reports that may be of interest to them. That is my application, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence is aware of everything that Ms. Kravetz presented, and we have no objection to these five documents that she proposed. We have another problem. It's a huge batch of documents and the Defence has not had enough time to go through all of them, especially since many of them are in English. We have to have them translated. And, if necessary, I should like to have your permission to tender some documents ourselves if the Prosecution does not have any objection. And since we have very little time, we would appreciate it if we could start our cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You haven't indicated the nature of these additional documents. I'm still leaping with you in your mind. First you say, We've got a big problem because we've been given a large number of documents therefore we want to add more documents. Now, I'm a little breathless keeping up with your mental process there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this Monday we were given notification that confidentiality has been lifted from State Department documents regarding KDOM reports, the US KDOM reports from 1998 and 1999. Ms. Kravetz selected five documents she wants to use relevant to the topics covered by this witness, and we have no objection to these. I believe I'm clear now. But since there is a large number of documents that have been made public now, we did not have enough time to go through all of those, and some of them we would certainly like to use. And we have had no time to put them on the list yet. That's all I meant. And, of course, it is Ms. Kravetz's agreement that we are seeking. This was not actually an application to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll take things in stages. Firstly, your motion to add the five documents to the list is granted. We will watch the time today with a point is reached or not whether it will be necessary to decide whether cross-examination should be delayed. And that too then will assist us with the further question of your own documents. But we appreciate your difficulty. Are we ready now for the witness, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I do have another matter, Your Honour. As Your Honours are aware, there will be a government representative in the courtroom today during the testimony of this witness. We just wanted to inquire with the Court regarding contact, if we are allowed to have contact with this US representative during the testimony of the witness. This was not made clear in the Chamber's decision, and I understand from discussion with this representative, her name is Ms. Karen Johnson that she way want to inform us of matters, if in any issues arises, that may be sensitive, she may want to draw our attention to that so we can alert the Court. So we would just want to receive some guide-lines as to how to proceed in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the proposal that the US government representative might speak to the Prosecution if some matter arises, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood that a representative of the US government is here to react to some questions that could pose a risk to confidentiality. And it's the American government that insisted on his [sic] presence here. What is important to me is that in view of the fact that confidentiality has been lifted from these facts and documents and these statements had been originally taken under Rule 70, I'm not sure whether the restrictions still stand on these topics. I thought it was up to the Trial Chamber to make the ultimate decisions whether a question falls within these topics and whether an answer is required regardless of what the US representative may insist on, correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the topics identified in the Annex A to our decision still apply. The decision which has made available to the public certain written records, which have now been provided to you apparently, is not one which alters the decision we have made about subjects that can be considered. The sole issue at the moment is whether the representative who is here of the provider may speak to the Prosecution if there is a concern that something the Prosecution wishes to do or is doing is leading into some area of difficulty. Ms. Kravetz is being careful to ensure that she doesn't upset you or us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understand that's why the representative of the government is here, and even if he [sic] is opposed to something, the Chamber will decide whether that falls within a certain topic or not, and the same will apply to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, Ms. Kravetz, it would be preferable if the representative of the government were able to speak with the witness; and the witness as a consequence if there's objection to providing information or answering a question, may then make that objection and that it would be preferable in the course of evidence if there was not any communication between the representative of the government and prosecuting counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine with us, Your Honour. I would just request that once the representative comes in the courtroom, she be informed that this is the procedure to be followed during this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's Ms. Johnson.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Karen Johnson, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, the next witness is Mr. Shaun Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Byrnes. Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you now. Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you now, Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that with you pursuant to our earlier order is Ms. Johnson as a representative of the government. Could I indicate, Ms. Johnson, to assist you, that your role is one which may probably best be conducted initially by you having conversation with the witness if some issue arises which concerns you. If there is objection to a question or something that is proposed, the witness should make that objection and you, of course, could consult with him before that occurs. Whether or not it will be necessary for any further submission about the matter, will depend on the circumstances. So if you would confine yourself to consultations with the witness and not, for example, with prosecuting counsel, I hope that will prove satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MS. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Byrnes, I believe Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, could you please begin by stating your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My full name is Shaun Michael Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Byrnes, that you are a retired officer from the United States foreign service?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In 1998, Mr. Byrnes, did you become involved in the work of a mission known as the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, also known as KDOM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, in April of 2007, did you provide testimony before this Tribunal in a case of Milutinovic et al. in relation to your work with the US KDOM mission?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I provided testimony in the case of Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to go over the transcript of your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed your testimony, if today you were asked the same questions that you were asked during the course of your testimony in that case, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this transcript. I understand that it's been assigned a provisional exhibit number of P1214. We would like it to be tendered under this exhibit number as a public exhibit. I wish to point out that there are some sections of this transcript which used to be under private -- or were initially private session due to a later order of the Milutinovic Chamber in relation to this transcript; the confidentiality with respect to those portions on the transcript was lifted. So we are tendering the whole of the transcript as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript will be received as an exhibit. Your electric personality is creating some problems, Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personality, Your Honours, has never before been described as electric, but I think proper measures have been taken, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, as this witness is a Rule 92 ter witness, I will proceed to read the in-court summary of his evidence. The witness was the head of the United States Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission from August 1998 until March 1999. He provides evidence on the role of this mission in Kosovo. He also provides evidence on the structure and chain of command of the VJ and MUP in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. During his tenure in Kosovo, Mr. Byrnes had meetings with the heads of sections of the VJ and the MUP and provides evidence on these meetings. He also speaks about the engagement of VJ and MUP units in operations in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. The witness recounts instances when he raised complaints with MUP general Lukic and other officials regarding the conduct of the MUP units during these operations. In October 1998, the witness led the negotiations with the MUP to agree on specific actions to be taken by FRY and Serbian forces to comply with UN Security Council Resolution 1199. He describes his negotiations and indicates that General Djordjevic chaired for the Serbian side. The witness also provides evidence on the Podujevo incident in December 1998 and on the Racak incident in January 1999. That is the end of the in-court summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, you had told us at the start of your testimony that you were involved in the work of the mission known as KDOM. Could you tell us -- could you please first start by explaining to the Chamber how it is that you became involved in the work of that mission?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I was asked by Washington in late July of 1998 if I would be willing to leave my current position as political minister councillor at our embassy in Rome to help stand up this mission which had been just recently agreed on. Washington was interested in having somebody with my background in Yugoslav and Balkan affairs. I had proper rank, and I was close. And so I agreed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when did you begin your work with this mission?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I believe I landed in Belgrade on August 10th, 1998. And after a day or two of orientation at our embassy there and which involved also meeting with a number of Serbian officials, I arrived in Pristina, Kosovo, on, I believe, the 12th of August and took command our Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was your mandate and what did your role entail of the US KDOM mission?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Our mandate was to provide accurate and objective information about what was occurring on the ground in Kosovo. This information was to be provided to Washington and the Contact Group capitals through our embassy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived in Kosovo on 12th of August in Pristina specifically. Just very briefly, can you describe what was the situation on the ground in Kosovo at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We were looking at an increasingly violent insurgency on the ground in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you elaborate. Exactly what was happening at the time? Why did Washington deem it necessary to set up this mission?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: If I may, let me -- let me add a little bit of context. Our mission grew out of an agreement made in mid-June in Moscow by Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic and then-president of the Russian Federation Boris Yeltsin. The agreement was intended by the Russians, I think, to try to head off another western intervention a la 1995 in Bosnia. It was intended to try to put a lid on growing violence between Albanian separatists and Serb security forces which was leading to the deaths of people on both sides, it was leading to increasing numbers of displaced persons, mostly Albanians but not always Albanians, and it was leading to growing western press attention which rest again a western intervention. The agreement provided for foreign observation, the hope was that this would lead to a diminishing of the violence and therefore provide time to seek a political solution. The violence, nevertheless, continued to grow. And my recollection -- I don't have the dates unfortunately, our special envoy for the Balkans, Richard Holbrooke, travelled to Belgrade in, I believe, early July to try to -- to meet with Milosevic to try to find a way of bringing this to a stop. They agreed at that point that the international community should be permitted to establish formal diplomatic observation missions. Holbrooke certainly knew that western embassies, the interested embassies, particularly the United States, Great Britain, France, Germany, and others, lacked the resources to provide observers on the ground in Kosovo on a sustained basis. In other words, they lacked the resources to make a difference. And they agreed therefore, to the establishment of three diplomatic observer mission: One would be American which I headed, a second would be a mission of the European Union, and the third was a Russian mission. That's what brought me there. Overall, our instructions were, again, to provide accurate, objective information on what was occurring. I think the hope was that by doing so pressure would be brought on both parties to restrain themselves. I think the ultimate objective was to buy time, to put the conflict, if you will, on hold and buy time so that a negotiated mutually acceptable political resolution could be found. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. Now, you have referred to the existence of three diplomatic observer missions. Was there any difference between these missions, the other two missions, and US KDOM; or did all three missions carry out the same type of mandate that you've described?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We all tried to carry out the same mission. The American mission had an advantage in that it was larger, it had more resources. The Russian mission never -- never was very large.
