I think at maximum it contained about five or six officers, and they lacked off-the-road vehicles. You needed off-the-road vehicles to work in areas where conflict was occurring. But we worked very closely. We -- the American -- the US KDOM worked very very closely with the EU counterpart and the Russian KDOM. I would add that the EU KDOM actually preceded the establishment of the KDOMs. The European Commission had established a monitoring mission in Kosovo in, I believe, April. And they had some 10 or 12 or 15 officers and vehicles on the spot. That -- it was headed by an Englishman. That EU monitoring mission or EC monitoring mission was simply renamed the EU KDOM and then they added additional resources to is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: By 12 August when you arrived in Pristina, was the US KDOM already functioning and operating, or did you get there to set it up, to carry out this task of setting it up?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, the European Union KDOM mission, I think that was your question, was already operating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was asking about the US, the United States KDOM mission.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood. Yes, the US KDOM -- the core of our mission had been established a couple of weeks earlier. We had a very small group of people, we had three or four off-the-road vehicles, and yes we were operating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have told us that your mandate was to provide accurate and objective information, how did you go about obtaining such information and carrying out this mandate?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We -- we ran daily patrols with our off-the-road vehicles into those parts of Kosovo where either there was ongoing conflict or we had reason to believe that there might be conflict. Are -- we had -- at that point we had three or four teams. Our teams consisted of two American officers and a local national interpreter. Local nationals were either Serb or Albanian. But in either instance, they had to be fluent in both languages. And that was not -- that was not a difficult condition for us to fulfill. So what we would do was we would usually launch our missions 8.00 in the morning, they would go to areas that we believed needed to be watched, where we might make a difference by getting in between the conflicting forces, and they would stay in those areas until nightfall. We were under instructions to be back at base by nightfall. Washington and Brussels did not want their people on the roads at night. We would stay in those areas, talk to people, collect information about what was going on, collect information about the humanitarian situation, about displaced people, that sort of thing. And then we would come back in, we would meet -- I would meet with the patrol leaders who would submit brief written reports, and then I or one of my other colleagues would put a report together which we faxed on a daily basis, usually late in the evening, to our embassy in Belgrade which then send it to Washington and to the other Contact Group embassies. Let me add that in this connection we worked very closely with the EU. Particularly in the beginning when both sides had limited resources and there seemed to be quite a bit of tension and even conflict occurring in Kosovo. I would meet every evening with my counterpart, an Englishman named Nicholas Turnbull; we would share our reporting from that day's activities, and we would discuss our expectations of what was likely to happen on the next day. And then we would divide up, because neither of us had enough people or enough vehicles to be everywhere. So we would, on a priority basis, decide where we would send our people, so we would avoid overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How would you obtain information of areas where there was ongoing conflict or that you thought should be particularly monitored?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Generally from our observation during the day, police movements, army movements, the International Red Cross had a mission there. UNHCR had a mission there. They were running teams into the field on -- for humanitarian purposes. We worked -- we stayed in touch with them. They would often tell us about build-ups of troops or villages being burned or that sort of thing. And we would often receive information from Albanian sources. People would call from villages wherever and say -- and tell us that there was a build-up of Serbian security forces in their area, and they were worried about what might happen the next day. So these were the basic sources of our information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you personally also participate in this sort of daily patrols as your mission was carrying on?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I did, but not every day. My rule of thumb was to go out twice a week. I felt it was important to do so so that I had a -- at least somewhat of a feel for what was going on in the field. And it was also a way, of course, of evaluating how my people were working, what were they doing, were they doing what they should have been, were they collecting, were they talking to the right kind of people. That sort of thing. Primarily it was so that I had a feel -- I was dealing with our ambassador in Belgrade, sometimes with the Contact Group ambassadors. I didn't want to have -- I didn't want to deal with them on the basis of second-hand information from my people. I wanted to have some personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you were not on the field participating in these patrols, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We were based in a suburb of Pristina called Kosovo Polje perhaps 6 kilometres south-west of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You spoke very briefly earlier about daily reports that you would compile and send to Washington and other organs -- other places. Could you tell us what sort of information would normally be included in these daily reports that your mission compiled?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The daily reports began with a general summary of the situation in the province of Kosovo, and then it had a section in which dealt with conflict situations, where we'd observe conflict, and briefly what had ensued. Then there was also a section, there was a humanitarian section which dealt with displaced persons. That information came both from our teams in the field who would come back and say, for example, Village of X had been attacked or subject to pressure from Serbian security forces, the population had left, the population was 1800 people, nobody is there now. That sort of thing. We also included information we received from the ICRC and UNHCR which, again, had teams in the field monitoring humanitarian situation. Washington and Brussels were interested in that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So would any important events that occurred during a specific day which -- regarding which you would obtain information, would these be always included in the daily reports that you would send to Washington and Brussels?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. If we were aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, during your work with the mission, did you have any contacts with local Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had considerable contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with officials from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who specifically were you in contact with?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My primary point of contact as chief of US KDOM was General Sreten Lukic who was the -- was in charge of the Serbian police forces in Kosovo. I -- because General Lukic was periodically absent in Belgrade, I also saw his deputy, it was a colonel named Mijatovic. I don't recall what his first name was. And then on a fairly regular basis, I would see the chief of the Kosovo Polje police department, his headquarters was down the street from where our, if you will, headquarters was established. He was good friends with the two Serbian brothers who owned the building we were in. It was a motel which had been converted into a sort of dormitory. And he was often down there for dinner. I got to know him, we talked. We had actually -- we had a very cooperative relationship with him. Those were the Serbian police officials that I would see regularly in Pristina. Of course, I -- when I made trips into the field, I often had contact with Serbian police officers there and I had some contact with the Serbian police officials when I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned that your primary point of contact was General Lukic. How frequently would you have meetings with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Very frequently. Often -- often daily. On some occasions when there was something serious going on, I would see him more than once a day. He -- let me add. He often would call me and ask me to come and see him. Most of the time I would -- it was at my request.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the nature of these meetings with General Lukic, what sort of topics would you discuss?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Well, the primary nature of the meetings was to discuss the security situation in the province and MUP compliance with the -- later on with the -- what we called the October Agreements. I would also use these meetings to raise objections or bring to his attention what we considered were unaccept -- from our standpoint unacceptable behaviour on the part of the Serbian police. And what I have in mind here is when villages were attacked, the inhabitants driven out and the villages burned after -- they were usually burned after the homes had been looted. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to meetings prior to the October Agreements and after the October Agreements were signed. These specific issues that you have just mentioned to attacks on villages and inhabitants being driven out, were these the subject of your meetings during which of the two periods or throughout the period there both before and after the October Agreements were signed?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The discussion of police behaviour was -- for the most part occurred prior to the October Agreements. The reason for that is that the October Agreements led to the establishment of OSCE's Kosovo Verification Mission which once it was stood up assumed the responsibilities that had originally been those of the KDOMs. And therefore the responsibility for dealing with compliance issues passed from Nick Turnbull, Sergey Lavrov, and myself, to William Walker and his staff at OSCE KVM.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to get into this topic in too much detail as it has already been addressed in your previous testimony. But just going back to your previous answer when you mentioned that you would raise complaints regarding behaviour that you considered unacceptable of the -- on the part of the Serbian police. When you would raise these complaints with General Lukic, what was generally his reaction to the issues that you were bringing to his attention?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Lukic generally rebuffed the complaints and my recollection was often attributed the actions his security forces had taken as the consequence of engagement with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you were out in the field during this period, and I'm speaking specifically about the period prior to the October Agreements, what sort of MUP units did you observe in the field, if any?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We saw -- we saw police units that were manning check-points on the roads, and they -- from our contact with these police they were -- they seemed -- my impression was they were regular Serbian police officers, for the most part seconded to Kosovo for 30 days, 30 days assignment, then they would return to their home city Kraljevo or Beograd or Novi Sad or wherever. These people manned the check-points. We also saw what we call the PJP which is Special Police, and they were dressed -- they were dressed differently and they appeared to be in an organised unit such as a military unit. In my previous testimony, I described them as light infantry, and that was our clear impression. These were not individual policemen put together to man a check-point or a roadblock. They were a coherent unit, had light infantry weapons including armoured cars, light anti-aircraft guns, heavy machine-guns, that sort of thing. They seemed to be in short a, at least, quasi-military formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were the tasks that you saw these PJP units performing in the field, was that at all different or -- from that of just regular police officers?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. My impression was that regular police officers served in effect in control functions, check-points, they provided security on the streets of Pristina and other large cities. The PJP units were used in, let's just say, anti-insurgency operations. They were used in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During your daily patrols or your routine patrols, did you have the opportunity of seeing PJP units in action?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: On one occasion which I related in my previous testimony, I saw a PJ unit which had just completed an operation in a village between the small town of Kijevo which was west of Pristina. And it was -- this village was located midway I think midway on a road running from Kijevo to the town of Malisevo and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say they had just completed an operation, what exactly were you able to observe taking place?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What I clearly still recall seeing in my mind's eye was arriving with a team at the edge of the village which was in flames. There was no -- there were no hostilities that we were aware of underway. We heard no sounds of gun-fire. There were a number of blue MUP buses parked at the edge of the village along with blue MUP trucks and several armoured personnel -- basically armoured scout cars. And what I remember is the MUP troops, if you will, with their weapons, coming out of the village and getting on to the buses and preparing to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in what condition was the village after these units had left?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The village was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to observe whether there was any civilian population in the village or the surrounding areas at the time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We -- other than the Serbian police, we saw nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you bring this specific incident that you were able to observe to the attention of General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was his explanation of what was taking place there, or did he provide any explanation?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To be honest, this was neither the first nor the last time I brought such incidents to his attention. This was a more personal intervention on my part because I had seen it with my own eyes, but to be frank, I do not remember precisely what he said in response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just a last question on this topic. When you would bring issues like this to the attention of Mr. Lukic, would you later observe any change in the actions of MUP units in the field, or would they just continue carrying out the same type of operations? Did you perceive your complaints as having any effect on what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My recollection, frankly, is no. And may I add a little comment here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: And that is, I quickly learned after arrival that with the MUP, not with the Yugoslav army, but with the MUP, our missions were playing basic cat and mouse games. Let me illustrate it with one quick anecdote. We initially ran missions Monday through Friday, and we would stand down on Saturday and Sunday to service our vehicles and just to give our stressed staff a break. We learned -- we learned very quickly that Yugoslav security -- or the Serbian security forces would often go to a low level of activity particularly towards the end of the week but then on Saturday and Sunday when we were not in the field they would go back into high gear and we would get reports from various sources that things were happening. Villages were being attacked or whatever. So Nick Turnbull and I decided we would run missions seven days a week and so we - as would make sense - we set up a schedule so we could still service our vehicles. And that seemed to change things a little bit, but it was very interesting and very challenging.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I want to move forward in time a bit to October 1998. You have mentioned the October Agreements. Did you have any involvement in negotiations that took place in October 1998 in Belgrade with Serbian officials to try to control the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: You are referring, madam, to the 24, 25, October talks in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I am specifically.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I was present -- I was present at those primarily in an expert capacity. The negotiations in effect involved two Working Groups. One which was headed by General Clark, and dealt with the regime under which the Serbian Yugoslav army, we called it the VJ, Vojska Yugoslavia, the regime under which the VJ would work once this agreement came into effect. The second Working Group dealt with the regime under which the Serbian police would work once the agreement came into effect. And on our side -- the -- our head of delegation was General Naumann a German was head at that time of the NATO Military Committee and who had accompanied General Clark to Belgrade for these meetings. I served in effect as his advisor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How is it that you became involved in these negotiations in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I was asked by General Clark and by Ambassador Holbrooke to participate because they wanted somebody on their team who had good knowledge of the situation on the ground in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The fundamental purpose of the negotiations was to stop the fighting and save lives. Secondary purpose was to allow for what we estimated to be about 200-, 250.000 displaced persons to return to their homes before the harsh winter set in. There was very great concern in New York at the United Nations and Brussels and in major European capitals and in Washington about an impending humanitarian disaster if the fighting continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, who from the Serbian police was -- participated in these negotiations in this second Working Group that you yourself was involved in?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I did not know all of the participants, but the officers that participated that I did know and recognised were General Djordjevic, General Lukic, General Stevanovic, and Colonel Mijatovic who was General Lukic's deputy was also present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you have already spoken about General Lukic and General Mijatovic. At the time, what did you understand to be General Djordjevic's position within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Djordjevic was the deputy minister of interior responsible for the -- for Serbia's public security forces. He was the deputy minister responsible for the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what about General Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Stevanovic was a deputy to General Djordjevic. My understanding when I arrived in Kosovo in August of 1998 was that he was the senior police official directly responsible for Kosovo. In other words -- and General Lukic was his deputy on the ground in Pristina. But at some point in the autumn, Lukic became formally responsible, he was the Serbian police commander in Pristina, in Kosovo. And General Stevanovic remained in Belgrade with whatever responsibilities he had. I, to be perfectly honest, never completely understood what his responsibilities were at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you understand to be the relationship between General Djordjevic and General Lukic? What was --

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Well, General Lukic was clearly General Djordjevic's subordinate and he reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During the conduct of these negotiations, what was the role of General Lukic? Did he have any specific role in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Lukic participated in the negotiations, but I do not recall him participating actively --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know if there was a problem with the transcript, maybe, but I said -- I was asking about the role of General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Djordjevic headed the Serbian team that dealt with the question of the regime the police would operate under in Kosovo once the October Agreement was put into effect. He was in charge of the -- of that working -- Serbian side of that Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And for how long did these negotiations last?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: They ran for a day and most of the next -- most of the ensuing night.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the -- what were the main points that you were negotiating about? What was the substance of the negotiations you were having with the MUP during this day and a half?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Basically we were negotiating definition of terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Specifically what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: What constituted a check-point, what constituted a -- even what constituted a road because if you look at the document, at least what I recall from that is - and I think this is in the document - the Serbian police were to be restricted to patrolling certain types of road, but they weren't -- the operational aspects. How do you implement the agreement. What are the rights, if you will, of the Serbian police under the terms of the agreement. We were trying to define them as precisely as we could so as to avoid problems of ambiguity which could lead to conflict and disagreement in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that General Djordjevic headed the Serbian MUP team. Were these points that you are referring to now issues that you were negotiating directly with him, or were you negotiating with one of the other members who were present there?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, General Djordjevic was the lead negotiator. What I recall is General Lukic would very occasionally be involved or say something, but General Djordjevic was clearly in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to have at this stage Exhibit P836 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This document will appear on the screen before you, Mr. Byrnes. Do you have the document there?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what it is?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: This is the document that was agreed at the end of these negotiations. This was the product, if you will, of the negotiations. It's an understanding between KDOM and the Ministry of Interior regarding the regime under which the Serbian security -- Serbian police in Kosovo would operate following the -- under the terms of the October Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that the document is signed by Colonel-General Djordjevic and also by you. Why is it that you are the person who signed for KDOM?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Clark and General Naumann wanted me to sign it because I was on the ground. General Naumann had negotiated this primarily, but he was not on the ground, he was in Brussels. They wanted somebody -- they wanted me to take responsibility for, in effect, ensuring that this document and this agreement was lived up to. And General Naumann simply could not do that in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this is why you were the person appointed to sign the agreement with General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, before I continue, Your Honours, I'm not sure when we are taking the next break or if there will be a next break since I know we are sitting on a different schedule today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are looking at the times, but I think we probably best use our time by going through in one session to about 1.30, which will be the limit of our tape, and then calling it the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 1 of the document that's there. We see it refers to the dismantlement of all check-points and it speaks about the establishment of 27 observation points on certain lines of communication. At the time, why was it considered necessary to dismantle all MUP check-points?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To permit displaced persons to return home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you understand to be -- when there's the reference here to 27 observation points, what did you understand what allowed of the MUP, what did you understand these observation points to mean?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Observation points were not to be check-points. If I may, let me say, check-points were, in effect, I would call them roadblocks. They were physical structures of a temporary nature placed on a road so that a vehicle or an individual travelling that road would have to stop. An observation point was to be precisely that. It was to be a physical structure of some sort. It could be a hole in the ground, if you will, but had to be off the road. The road had to be unobstructed and open to free passage of vehicles and individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during the course of these negotiations, did you have the impression that General Djordjevic was aware or had sufficient information about the areas in Kosovo where MUP units were deployed?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: General Djordjevic demonstrated a very clear knowledge of the facts on the ground in Kosovo. He was clearly a professional. He took his job as deputy -- as head of the police, deputy minister of interior seriously, and he knew down to detail what was going on and where his people were and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there anything specific that was discussed during these negotiations that gave you that impression, that he had such detail about where his people were and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. Discussions about locations of observation points, how close to the roads they would be, potential flash-points that he was concerned about. This -- General Djordjevic had -- very frankly, had a professional's command of the facts. He was on top of his brief, and he was a very tough negotiator.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: He was on top of his brief. The sort of thing that General Clark and General Naumann was pushing for would, from an objective standpoint, would clearly impede the ability of General Djordjevic's policemen to go after the KLA. This put -- these restrictions were real constraints on the ability of the Serbian police to actively engage the KLA. From his standpoint, he was dealing with an insurgency and I -- I can -- I understand now and I understood then why he would want to defend to the maximum extent or preserve to the maximum extent his flexibility to deal with situations as they might arise. He was a very -- he was very tough in negotiating these issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While these negotiations were ongoing, were you provided any information by General Djordjevic or by other members of the MUP delegation as to the number of MUP personnel in Kosovo at the time? And we're talking end of October.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To be very honest, I simply do not remember. During the course of the negotiations, I just don't have a memory of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this discussed at all, the numbers of MUP personnel that would be allowed in Kosovo after the conclusion of this agreement? Was this a matter of discussion?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It certainly was, and that's reflected in one of the other documents that was agreed, or -- if I can add, there was discussion and agreement on a number of Serbian police that could remain in the province and the number of VJ units and their equipment that could remain in the province.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during the course of these negotiations at any time did General Djordjevic have to consult with anyone before reaching an agreement with you or the other international negotiators on issues to be included in this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I personally never saw him consult outside the room in which we were working. But he did leave the room on a number of occasions. I can only presume that it was for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have Exhibit P837 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe the witness could also be shown the second page of the document in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically this was a document reflecting the results of the negotiations held on 24 and 25 October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down on the second page to Roman numeral II, paragraph 1, we see that it says: "With these goals in mind the state authorities of the FRY have announced the following measures." And number one says: "Special units deployed to Kosovo after February 1999 [sic] will be withdrawn from Kosovo." Do you recall why the date of February 1999 [sic] was chosen as a date to include in this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It was chosen because there was a big build-up of Serbian security forces, the police, and the army after -- in March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in your understanding, were special units allowed to remain -- were there any special units that were allowed to remain in Kosovo after the conclusion of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: My understanding -- my memory is that the Special Police units were to be withdrawn from Kosovo. But as I look at this document at page 2.1 under Roman numeral II I see the statement: "Combined police/special police strength in Kosovo will be reduced to February 1998 duty level." And that suggests to me that there was a provision allowing the Special Police -- some Special Police to remain in the province provided it was not more than -- their numbers were not more than they were in February 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At the time, did you have that information of what the numbers were prior to February 1998? Was this information that was provided to you by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The MUP provided us with information. However, we had no idea whether that was accurate information. We had no clear idea, in my recollection, as to what MUP strength was in February 1998. We simply didn't have a yard-stick.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, top paragraph of the next page in the English, paragraph 2. And in the B/C/S I think we need to remain in the same page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 2 it refers to additional heavy weapons or equipment brought into Kosovo or transferred from the VJ to police or Special Police units, and it says that this will be withdrawn from Kosovo, returned to the VJ. Why was it necessary to include such a provision in this agreement, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: To enable the police to return to traditional police functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this a specific issue that you were aware of that heavy weapons were being transferred from the VJ to police or Special Police units for their operations? Was this an issue of concern at this time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It was indeed because the Special Police units that we observed in the field often had equipment with them, heavy weapons that we did not normally assume a police unit would have. And I'm talking about mortars, I'm talking about armoured -- not only armoured scout cars but armoured personnel carriers and light anti-aircraft weapons mounted on trucks or armoured vehicles. Those are not -- that's not equipment that most observers, I believe, would consider as part and parcel of a police inventory. And, of course, our concern was that this equipment was being used against the population. We were anxious to see people return from the fields and the woods and the mountains to their villages and concern was that if they saw police units with this kind of weaponry, they would be much more hesitant about going back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this an issue that was discussed during your negotiations with General Djordjevic or was it discussed in a wider frame?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the MUP position at the time regarding the use of heavy weaponry and the transfer of heavy weaponry from the VJ to the police, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Well, as the document shows, they agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: They agreed to the withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: They signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 5. I know you were not involved in the negotiations with the VJ, but we see that here with regard to the VJ there's a reference to all VJ elements remaining in Kosovo or returned to garrison except three company-sized teams. And there are certain lines of communication that are indicated there. Do you have any information as to why these specific lines of communication included in this agreement and why these company-sized teams were allowed to be deployed along these communication lines?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes. In brief, the VJ was permitted to establish these outstations, these deployments, in order to protect key roads through which they were reinforced, supplied, and basically which they travelled. These were roads that from a local perspective had strategic importance. They argued that the KLA, which was armed, threatened them and if these roads were cut off, their units would be isolated. That is the reason they were allowed to establish these deployments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, moving away from the document, after these agreements were concluded, did you return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was your role then after the conclusions of these agreements? Did it remain the same as in the earlier months or did it change in any way?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It changed only in the sense that Nick Turnbull and I, Nick Turnbull of the EU KDOM were designated stand-ins for the new OSCE KVM mission which had been agreed but had to be established. So our responsibilities were to monitor the implementation of the October Agreement until such time as OSCE KVM was in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say "monitor the implementation" of the agreements, was your role to deal specifically with the MUP or did you have to deal both with the VJ and the MUP in the monitoring of the compliance of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It wasn't just monitoring complaints, it was monitoring the draw down of VJ units and withdrawal of the Special Police, for example, from the province. It was to monitor the full implementation of the agreement. And, yes, we did have to deal with the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings with General Djordjevic after the conclusion of the agreement that we saw earlier in relation to the compliance of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't remember precisely. I know -- what I remember is I -- I was a participant in a fairly large meeting in Pristina in which he participated and Ambassador William Walker, who was head of the OSCE KVM mission, and again it was get acquainted, let's go over what our responsibilities are, what our obligations are to one another. I remember that meeting. On our side, Bill Walker was the point man. It must have occurred after the agreement, but unfortunately I can't give you a date. And it was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall who participated at this meeting? You said it was a fairly large meeting in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I remember from our side it was myself, Nicholas Turnbull from the EU KDOM, it was General -- William Walker, his aid Colonel Michael Phillips, the British head of -- the British deputy director, deputy head of KVM OSCE who was deputy head for operations General Drewienkiewicz, those are -- on our side those are faces I remember. On their side: Nikola Sainovic, Veljko Dalovic, who was the prefect for -- basically the head of the Pristina municipality, and General Djordjevic. I honestly can't remember if General Lukic was there, it would make sense that he was, but I don't have a clear recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have referred to Nikola Sainovic, what at the time did you understand to be Mr. Sainovic's position?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was first deputy prime minister and had as part of his duties he had -- he had responsibility for Kosovo. Within the government, he was the point man on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have any subsequent contacts with him or was this the only occasion when you met with Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I had a fair amount of contact with Mr. Sainovic over the months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And generally what was the nature of this meetings you had or contacts you had with Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: It was generally the consequence of problems we had in the field, you might say crises, there were periodic crises. Each time we -- each time we had a crises, for example, the capture of eight VJ soldiers by the KLA, there was a risk that this would provoke serious violence, and that, of course, put at risk the October Agreement and our efforts to calm things down so a political solution could eventually be found. Sainovic was interested from his standpoint trying to find a resolution to crises. And over time, as our relationship developed, he expressed an interest in -- and even meeting privately with KLA leaders in an effort to explore the possibilities of some sort of broader agreement, truce, unfortunately we never were able to get that far.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you understand Mr. Sainovic at the time to have any sort of authority over the units that were deployed in the field, and I'm speaking about VJ and MUP units. Did understand him to have any authority over these units?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Only in the sense that Mr. Sainovic represented the political side of the government. I never had the sense that he could personally order the police or the military to do -- to take specific action. But again, let me stress, that's an impression, I was not on the inside, I didn't attend their meetings, I didn't have documents. And my impression is clearly influenced by my own experience as -- I served as a navy officer years ago and then as a foreign service officer, so I'm clearly influenced by the way our system works.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you perceive him to have any influence on events in the grounds --

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- when you would raise a complaint with him, could he influence what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how was that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The clearest anecdote I can give you is going back to the case of the eight VJ soldiers who were captured. We worked directly with Sainovic to find -- to cut a deal, to find a way to get these people free. The KLA was simply not going to let them go because Bill Walker or Shaun Byrnes or anybody else from the international community went to them and said please let them go. They weren't going do that. So it was with Sainovic that we dealt with an order to put together something, and that something involved basically a prisoner exchange. And he was the guy, he was the fellow that made it happen. He clearly -- clearly he had influence. I don't think General Lukic could have done that. I mean, that was fundamentally a political decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And have Exhibit 05346 up on the screen. If only the English could be displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have the document before you, Mr. Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: This is a copy of the -- one of our daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that this is dated December 19th, 1998. I understand from your answer that at the time you were still producing daily reports up until -- at this period you were still producing daily reports?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the first paragraph, it refers to fragile cease-fire that came under further pressure as the VJ deployed an armoured battle group to the Podujevo region, and in paragraph 2 of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Kravetz. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we received some kind of version of this translation, and for the accused to be able to follow I would like the B/C/S version to be put up. I myself cannot follow very well, although I have it on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I had only requested for the the English to be displayed for the witness, but of course for the Court -- we can't do that. Okay. That's fine. If we could zoom in then a bit more on the document, second paragraph in the English just so the witness is able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, if the witness cannot see, well, now that the screen is split, then it's all right with us, you can keep the English version on the screen alone and I'll give the accused the translation on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's being brought up as much as we can, and I think he should be able to follow it in the Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I had asked for the second paragraph of the first page to be displayed, not the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to paragraph 2 of this document, we see that it says: "The VJ told KDOM that the armoured battle group which moved into the area of Podujevo early today was a 'training exercise' VJ officials had failed to notify KDOM of the movement, in violation of the Kosovo verification agreement." Do you recall the incident to which this report is referring to in the area of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on your recollection, what took place there at this time? We are speaking of the period of 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: The army moved a company-sized battle group from the Marshal Tito barracks in Pristina to an area east of Podujevo. The convoy included Serbian police and Serbian police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of this event, that this was occurring?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: We observed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Where were your observers at the time? Where were they based when they observed this deployment?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: I don't remember precise locations, but what I can tell you is that OSCE KVM maintained observation posts in proximity to the entrance and egress points of the Yugoslav army's bases or garrisons. So they monitored, as they were required to and permitted to under the agreement, they monitored the movement in and out of garrison of VJ movements -- VJ vehicles. Later on after this battle group had moved into position in the Podujevo area, I placed one of our vehicles right at the gate of the encampment that they established. So we kept very close eye on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did anyone within the KDOM or KVM at the time contact VJ officers to find out what was happening, why this deployment was occurring?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Let me stress here that KVM -- OSCE KVM was up and operating by this time and they had taken over responsibility for dealing with the Serbian authorities in Kosovo on implementation issues. So they dealt specifically, officially, and formally with the Serbian authorities. My recollection is that Bill Walker sent General Drewienkiewicz to deal with his counterpart on this specific incident and Drewienkiewicz stayed in touch with this fellow. It may have been General Loncar, I can't recall directly. But Drewienkiewicz was in direct contact with his Serbian counterpart throughout the period in which this incident unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see from the document that the VJ -- the information received from -- by KDOM from the VJ was said that this was a training exercise. And it's put in quotes in the document, is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Because that's a direct quote; that's what they told us when we asked them about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this document at this stage. It's 05346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01246.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have 05347 up on the screen. If we could zoom in on paragraphs 1 and 2 on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we see that this is another daily report. It's dated December 20th, 1998, a day after the one we just saw earlier. And we see in paragraph 1 there's a reference to KDOM and KVM monitoring the activities of the VJ armoured battle group undertaking a training exercise near Podujevo; and in paragraph 2, there's a reference to the continued deployment and an indication of the type of vehicles and personnel deployed, and the last sentence says "the group's exercise include sending heavily armed patrols along the Podujevo-Pristina road." Now, at the time, this is the day after you had been told that this was a training exercise, when these deployments were observed by your observers, were you still under the impression that the VJ was deploying these units to the area to conduct training or did you have any information as to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: Our very distinct impression at the time was that this was not an exercise and that it was being done to protect the most strategic road linking Kosovo with Serbia. The road between Pristina-Podujevo went on to cross the border into Serbia proper, and then went on to Nis which was the headquarters of the -- I believe it was the Yugoslav 3rd Army. That's where -- and I would add that parallel to the road ran a rail line, the only major rail line running into Kosovo. On those two communications links depended the Serbian security forces supplies and of course other things. These roads and this railroad were important for the movement of civilians and commerce and trade. So it was very important to Belgrade that they be kept open. The road had come under increasing pressure from the KLA in the area. I don't know if that's reflected in this report, I don't recall, but the KLA commander in the Lap region was very aggressive, was not particularly interested in fulfilling the terms of the October Agreement to which of course the KLA was not party. Our job and then Bill Walker's job in large part had been to sell this agreement to the KLA, to get them to play by the agreement's rules. This fellow had begun to move his troops closer to the road and there had been incidents along the road in the period leading up to this. In short, this was the response of the Yugoslav -- of the Serbian security forces. This was a critical strategic link and they had -- they had to defend it. They had to keep it open.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we saw earlier when we were looking at one of the agreements signed in October that company-sized teams were authorised along certain lines of communication. Was the Pristina-Nis road -- Podujevo-Pristina-Nis road included? I mean, were units allowed to be deployed along that axis?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES
utterances.text: No, it was not. I've looked at the documents to prepare for this, and it was not included. And I have to say ten years later or 11 years later, I have to wonder about that omission. I don't have any information on that because that -- those deployments and the regime which governed the behaviour, if you will, of the Serbian army was negotiated by the other Working Group led by General Clark. I wasn't party to it. And we were up all night negotiating these documents after which Slobodan Milosevic treated us to a brunch and then everybody got on airplanes and left. I'm sorry for being long-winded, but I just don't know. I -- from a strategic standpoint, I don't understand why the Serbian army wasn't allowed to have a battle group up there to protect a strategic -- clearly the most important strategic line of communication. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see, Your Honours, that it's already 1.30. Before we break, I would like to tender this document, 05347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01247.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a convenient time to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have run out of the time we can run on our tapes, Mr. Byrnes, and we must adjourn although it's a quarter of an hour before our normal time as we've had a disrupted programme today. We resume this trial tomorrow at 9.00, and we would ask that you be back for that. The Court Officer will assist you with any further details that you need in the interim. And no doubt Ms. Johnson with you. So we adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.
